messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arjun Patel was 20 when his older cousin, who had helped raise him after the family immigrated to the United States, died suddenly in a car accident. Arjun had spoken to him that afternoon about ordinary things—what to cook that weekend, a draft Arjun was working on, whether they might visit relatives over the summer. By evening, his aunt was screaming into the phone. What stayed with Arjun was not only the fact of the death but the speed with which an ordinary day had split open. Someone could be joking with you at four o’clock and gone by dinner. In the weeks afterward, that became the lesson he took from it: the world was not stable or fair, and whatever assumptions he had once had about life unfolding in some understandable way felt ruined. He had been, by his own account, an easygoing and hopeful person; now he told himself that version of him was gone, replaced by someone who was miserable all the time and could not trust life at all.

Those beliefs began to organize how he moved through each day. Because he had come to see the world as fundamentally dangerous and unpredictable, making plans felt naive, almost superstitious, as if setting up a future only invited it to be taken away. He stopped agreeing to trips, deadlines beyond the bare minimum, even casual plans with friends. As a writer, he had once liked sketching out long projects and imagining where he might be in a year; now he avoided thinking past the current day. He also found himself repeatedly texting his mother, friends, and sometimes his aunt with variations of the same question—was he okay, did he seem normal, was this going to pass—because he no longer trusted his own mind to tell him he was safe. He began steering away from anything that reminded him of his cousin: family photos, certain foods they had shared, discussions about weddings or travel, even passages in his own writing that touched grief or loss. To Arjun, this withdrawal made sense. If happiness had already been taken once, then hoping, remembering, and looking ahead all felt dangerous.

At the same time, those same shattered beliefs kept his body in a constant state of alarm. He said that if death could arrive in the middle of an ordinary day, then nowhere really counted as safe, even his bedroom. He could be sitting at home knowing logically that nothing was happening and still feel unable to relax, as if his body were waiting for the next phone call. Ordinary sounds—a car door slamming outside, a phone buzzing sharply on the desk, a pan dropped in the kitchen—made him jolt. Nights were the worst. Sleep had become difficult because lying still in the dark left too much room for the thought that life could change irreversibly at any moment, without warning and without reason.

Over the following months, the ways he tried to manage this only deepened what he believed about himself and the world. Avoiding reminders of his cousin gave him brief relief, but it also meant his loss stayed frozen as something unbearable, something that could not be approached without collapse. Each time he canceled plans or refused to imagine the future, he felt more convinced that happiness was over for him and that the world really was too dangerous to trust. The repeated reassurance seeking helped for a few minutes at most. Soon he would need to ask again, which left him feeling even less steady, as though if other people stopped answering he would fall apart. His life narrowed around these habits. He wrote alone at odd hours to avoid conversations, missed informal meetings with other young writers, and turned down opportunities that required committing himself in advance.

Those same strategies also fed the sense of threat that now dominated his days. Because he kept organizing his life around avoiding reminders and scanning for signs that something might go wrong, his nervous system never seemed to settle. In his small apartment, a notification sound from his laptop could make him jump hard enough to spill coffee over his notes. When an editor asked to schedule a call the following week, his first impulse was to decline rather than sit with the unease of anticipating anything. The more he avoided, the more fragile safety felt; the more he sought reassurance, the less he could relax once he was alone again. Sleep became more disrupted, and exhaustion made him feel even more on edge.

He finally sought help after his mother pointed out that he was living as though another catastrophe were always minutes away. Arjun was frightened by how small his life had become at 20, and by the thought that if he kept going like this he would lose not only his cousin but any sense of a future. What he wanted most was not to forget the death, but to stop feeling that the world had ended with it and that any plan, any moment of calm, was only setting him up to be shattered again.
